title: Copper Contact and Spirit Character | Craft Beer School
desc: Why pot stills are made of copper and how copper contact removes sulphur from new make spirit, with the design and running choices that change it.
teaser: Copper is not tradition for its own sake. It is a chemical filter that takes sulphur out of the spirit.
standfirst: Pot stills are copper because copper reacts with sulphur compounds and removes them from the spirit. How much copper the vapour touches and how fresh that copper is both change the character of the new make.
sections:
A fermented wash carries sulphur compounds made by the yeast. Some smell of struck matches, rotten eggs, cabbage or rubber. Copper reacts with many of them and holds them on its surface, so they never reach the spirit. Copper also conducts heat well and can be shaped by hand, which is why coppersmiths have built pot stills from it for centuries.

A stainless steel pot still would make a spirit with much more sulphur. Some modern stills use steel for parts that the vapour does not touch, but the parts in contact with vapour and spirit are normally copper.

Copper works best on vapour. The most active zones are the upper pot, the neck, the lyne arm and the condenser. Liquid that refluxes passes over the copper again, so a still with more reflux gives more contact. In the condenser, the spirit is liquid and the surface area depends on the condenser type.

Shape sets the amount. Tall necks, boil balls and rising lyne arms increase contact. Short necks, falling lyne arms and worm tub condensers reduce it. See lyne arm angle and spirit character and our guide to worm tubs versus shell and tube condensers.

Copper does not work forever without rest. As it reacts with sulphur, its surface becomes coated. A still run hard and continuously loses some of its effect. Many distilleries leave stills open between runs so air can reach the copper and refresh the surface, a practice often called resting the still. Running more slowly also helps, because vapour spends more time in contact with copper.

The copper itself is slowly consumed. Over years, the walls of the neck, lyne arm and condenser wear thin, especially where vapour hits hardest. Stills need regular inspection and eventually patched or replaced sections.
What more or less copper tastes like

High copper contact gives a cleaner, lighter new make, often fruity or floral, with little sulphur. Low copper contact leaves more sulphur, which can give the new make a meaty, heavy or slightly vegetal character. That is not always a fault. Some sulphur fades during maturation. A heavier spirit can develop depth in cask. Distilleries that want a robust style deliberately limit copper contact.

Too much sulphur in the new make, though, can linger in the whisky for years. Our guide to copper levels in spirit covers the other side: how much copper ends up dissolved in the spirit itself.
Running choices that change copper contact

The stillman has a few levers:

  • Heating rate. A slow run gives more contact and more reflux.
  • Rest between runs. Letting air reach the copper refreshes its surface.
  • Charge level. A lower charge leaves more neck space for vapour to touch copper.
  • Condenser temperature. Warmer condensing can increase copper contact in some designs.

Small changes in these show up in the new make. Record them for every run, alongside the cut points.

Change one lever at a time. If you slow the run and rest the still on the same day, you will never know which one cleaned up the spirit. Copper effects are also slow to read, because new make can smell different after a few days in a sample bottle as some sulphur notes fade.

Craft distilleries in India often commission stills from local coppersmiths, which makes copper contact a design choice you can make on purpose. Ask the fabricator about copper thickness in the neck and lyne arm, because those wear fastest. Indian cooling water is often warm, which can push a distillery to run stills harder to keep throughput up. That cuts copper contact. Plan condenser capacity so you are not forced to choose between output and spirit quality.

The whole system interacts: still shape, condenser, running speed and the sulphur coming in from the washback. Understanding those links is the core of a distilling course. They are also the reason no single setting fixes a sulphury spirit.
A first test on your own still

Run two spirit still charges from the same low wines. Distil one at your normal heating rate and the other noticeably slower, with everything else the same. Keep the heart cuts separate, reduce both to about 20% ABV with water and nose them side by side for sulphur. The difference tells you how much your copper is doing.
faqs: Why are whisky stills made of copper?
Copper reacts with sulphur compounds in the vapour and removes them, giving a cleaner spirit. It also conducts heat well and is easy to shape.
Does more copper contact make better whisky?
It makes a lighter, cleaner spirit. Some distilleries limit copper contact on purpose for a heavier, more robust style.
What does resting a still mean?
Leaving the still open to air between runs so the copper surface refreshes and works better on the next run.
Yes. Copper is slowly consumed by the reactions, so necks, lyne arms and condensers need inspection and eventual repair.
